biography_sections.markdown:
{{figure:family-network.svg}}

The Lisnagaver evidence supports a local Glasgow network; it does not yet yield a single reconstructed pedigree. The starting point is the 1851 sequence. [House 34](https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Rasharkin/Lisnagaver/34/) contains John Glasgow, farmer, with wife Margaret and his unmarried brother Samuel, a linen weaver. [House 35](https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Rasharkin/Lisnagaver/35/) contains Alexander and Mary with their children. [House 37](https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Rasharkin/Lisnagaver/37/) contains Thomas Glasgow and Mary Ann. A Watters household separates Alexander and Thomas. The layout establishes a small same-surname farming cluster and useful geographic proximity; enumeration order is not a kinship statement or a property map.

John `Glasgow-867` and Samuel `Glasgow-2908` belong to a specific **father-John branch**. John’s [original 16 November 1846 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063) names his father as John Glasgow, farmer. The 1851 household expressly calls Samuel John’s brother. That chain directly establishes the brotherhood and names John-867’s father and his occupation. Extending that father statement to Samuel assumes they shared a father; the census does not distinguish full from half brothers. It does **not** identify that father with John `Glasgow-1022`, the older Glenleslie man, and it does not make Alexander another son. The corrected memorial/death identification is 1885 aged 78, implying birth about 1806–07; the former 1895-based age objection is superseded. The 1851 census age implies an earlier birth about 1801. Neither age identifies his father with Glenleslie John. Any maintained attachment to John-1022 is an uncertain identification of the father, not an additional record and not evidence for Alexander’s parentage.

The distinction matters because the neighbouring tenancy pattern is tempting but not decisive. The 1834 tithe names Alexander and Robert Glasgow at Lisnagaver, while later valuation lots 24, 25 and 26 are associated with John, Alexander and Thomas under Robert Harvey. Acreage, field-book and adjacency arguments can suggest tenancy succession or a broader network. They cannot establish a biological descent, and Plantation-measure tithe acreage cannot be numerically matched to statute-measure valuation acreage to manufacture an inheritance. The 1836 field book names Robert Glasgow and Archibald McCaughan junior in the house section but does not name Alexander; its land section does not supply occupier names. It therefore cannot decide who lived together, who inherited, or whether Alexander was a brother of John or Thomas.

Thomas `Glasgow-987` and Daniel `Glasgow-3896` have a stronger relationship argument than Alexander has with either. Daniel’s 1871 will, indexed through the [PRONI Wills Calendar](https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx), calls the late Thomas his brother and identifies Daniel Neely Glasgow as nephew; Daniel Neely’s [28 June 1888 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1888/10763/5925382.pdf) in turn names Thomas Glasgow, farmer, as his father. Those two records establish Daniel and Thomas as brothers. Thomas’s [PRONI calendar administration](https://apps.proni.gov.uk/WillsCalendar_IE/WillsSearch.aspx) adds that the Lisnagaver farmer died 21 June 1870 and administration went to widow Mary Anne on 7 September. It was an intestate administration, not a will, and it names no parent, sibling or heir beyond the widow. It cannot be used to extend the proved brotherhood into a parentage for Alexander.

Alexander may be a brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel. Shared locality, associated land, church context and descendant testimony make that a worthwhile research model. No confirmed Y-DNA comparison with an independently documented Thomas or Daniel descendant is supplied in this case. None of those sources says that Alexander was their brother, so the three men are not a proved sibling set. The 2020 correspondence records the older Alexander-and-Rosanna belief, but provides no demonstrably independent parentage source: the correspondent said she *believed* Thomas’s parents were Alexander and Rosanna, separately wondered whether the user’s Alexander was Thomas’s brother, and supplied neither a record citation nor usable autosomal-match data. The later FamilySearch Pedigree Resource File entries derive from an Ancestry member tree and conflict even on Rosanna’s reported death day. They show the circulation of a tradition, not its verification.

### The Irish–Canadian family: what the original deeds establish

The Canadian connection is now supported by an explicit transaction. In the [registered deed of **30 July 1861**, B465](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWB8-D), **Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, County Londonderry, watchmaker**, and **Thomas Glasgow, farmer of the County Antrim townland written Lislagaver/Lisnagaver**, sell Samuel Glasgow of Prescott two undivided sixths of the Centre Street property. Their wives are **Margaret** and **Mary Anne**, and the deed expressly derives the interests from Robert Glasgow's will. Place, occupation, wives and the already proved Daniel–Thomas brotherhood identify these men with [Daniel-3896](/people/glasgow-3896.html) and [Thomas-987](/people/glasgow-987.html). This resolves the former uncertainty about whether the will's Irish brothers were the known Kilrea and Lisnagaver men.

Robert's [will of **9 October 1849**, B12](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWY9-S), registered in 1856, gives one sixth each to brothers **Daniel, Samuel, John and Thomas**, one sixth to sister **Mary**, and one sixth collectively to **the children of brother James**. Combined with B465, this places Daniel and Thomas in the same documented sibling group as [Samuel of Prescott-4010](/people/glasgow-4010.html) and Robert. The original does **not** call James deceased: the earlier death-before-1849 inference is withdrawn. It names no parents.

| Original record | People, property and transaction | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [B12, 9 October 1849; registered 13 November 1856](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWY9-S), DGS 008200419, images 35–36, pp.9–10 | Robert's six shares, including one collectively for brother James's children. Executors Alexander McWilliam and Samuel Glasgow. | Direct sibling wording. Alexander Glasgow witnesses the 1856 registration request; that is a different role from beneficiary. James's death is not stated. |
| [B13, 30 October 1856](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWYM-6), image 36, pp.10–11 | **John Glasgow, Prescott watchmaker, and wife Jane** sell Samuel, merchant, **one sixth for £125**; Jane releases dower. Registered 13 November. | An actual acquisition of a share. John's trade also gives a specific occupational comparison with his brother Daniel. |
| [B395, 23 November 1860](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWR4-5), image 208, pp.336–337 | **Eliza Jane Glasco**, Rochester, New York, spinster, eldest daughter of **James Glasco, formerly of Prescott, carpenter**, sells Samuel **one ninth for £33 6s 8d**. Registered 22 December. | Explicit father–daughter relationship and residence. No explicit derivation from Robert's will. The copied registration signature says James although the grantee is Samuel. |
| [B465, 30 July 1861](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWB8-D), images 240–241, pp.397–398 | **Daniel and Margaret of Kilrea; Thomas and Mary Anne of Lisnagaver**; two sixths to Samuel for **$1,000 Canadian currency**, expressly under Robert's will; executed at Coleraine. | The direct Irish identification and inheritance link. The official abstract gives registration 7 October 1861. The deed opening and closing copy differ on the July day; the opening date is used here. |
| [B601, 27 June 1863](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWBS-7), image 316, pp.542–543 | **Mary Glasco**, Rochester spinster, second eldest daughter of **James, formerly Prescott carpenter**, sells Samuel **one ninth for £33 6s 8d**. **Alexander Glasgow of Prescott, gentleman**, witnesses. Registered 3 August. | Identifies a second daughter of the carpenter. It does not identify the witness as Alexander-951 or explicitly describe the interest as a share under Robert's will. |

These deeds concern **Lot 12 south of Dibble Street and a 3,400-square-foot part of Lot 11**, the house at **388 Centre Street**. The [municipal designation report](https://www.prescott.ca/media/3dtiztjk/council-agenda-june-16-2025.pdf), printed pp.31–32, and the [2017 property account](https://www.theresataylor.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Auction-all-for-others-Brockville-Recorder.pdf) agree on 388. The former 280 reference was a project citation error. [OnLand's official parcel search](https://www.onland.ca/ui/15/property/address) identifies PIN **68159-0153**, Plan 19, Block 2; the [historical abstract, p.71](https://www.onland.ca/ui/15/books/48793/viewer/998408458?page=97), connects the same Lot 11 strip to Robert's **5 April 1841** purchase from Susannah Jessup. Samuel's **251 Water Street West**, Plan 19, Block 2, part Lot 16, remains a separate property.

### James's family: a promising identification with an unresolved title problem

Eliza Jane and Mary are explicitly sisters and daughters of **James the Prescott carpenter**. Identifying that James with Robert's brother is a strong property-based hypothesis, because both daughters convey interests in the same two parcels to Samuel. It is not yet proved by an express kinship or inheritance clause. Each daughter's **one-ninth** interest is also recorded in the official abstract. Together they exceed the **one-sixth** collective share given to James's children in Robert's will. Earlier ownership, additional inherited interests or a record error must be examined before treating these as a simple distribution of that sixth. The fractions cannot responsibly supply a child count.

The **1868 Alexander deed has now been inspected**. [C114, 25 March 1868](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRC-Y), DGS 008200420, image 120, pp.164–165, identifies **Alexander Glasco of Rochester, Monroe County, New York, express agent, son of James Glasco formerly of Prescott, carpenter**. Through attorney Macneil Clarke he conveys **one eighteenth** for **$166.66** to **Mary Eno Glasgow, widow of the late Samuel Glasgow**. The [accompanying C113 power of attorney](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRK-B) was made at Rochester on **28 December 1867**; both instruments were registered on **18 August 1868**. The abstract's August date is therefore registration, not the deed's execution date.

This positively identifies a son of James the carpenter alongside Eliza Jane and Mary. It supplies **three named children**, without claiming a complete family or resolving how their title shares arose. It identifies a Rochester express agent, not a Lisnagaver farmer: linking him to Alexander-951 would require an independent wife, age, birthplace or migration bridge. No such bridge was found in this inspection, so this father statement is not assigned to Alexander-951. The earlier Prescott witness named Alexander is a relevant comparison, but the shared name does not prove he was the express agent either. **Mary Eno** is the widow's recorded name; the document does not establish Eno as a maiden surname.

### Mary Glasgow Black and the Drumoolish connection

The [original **C298 deed of 15 September 1869**](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQTY-K), registered **1 July 1870**, explicitly identifies **Mary Black, formerly Mary Glasgow, as sister of the late Robert Glasgow of Prescott**. It names her six children and conveys the family’s interest to Samuel’s widow for **$800**. This is another direct Irish bridge: two of the children reside at **Drumoolish, County Londonderry**. The deed gives a record-based family to compare with the wider Bann Valley and Inishrush evidence; it does not name Mary’s parents or make her a daughter of Adam.

| Child of Mary Glasgow Black | Residence and description in the deed | Spouse or estate detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| John Black | Drumoolish, County Londonderry; yeoman | Wife Martha joins. |
| Rose Ann Black | Drumoolish; spinster | Living party. |
| Jane Miller | Newburgh, Orange County, New York | Wife of Robert Miller. |
| Agnes Black | Newburgh; spinster | Living party. |
| Thomasina Montgomery | Legrand, Marshall County, Iowa | Wife of Mathew Montgomery. |
| Elizabeth Black | Newburgh; spinster | Had died unmarried and intestate; the five named siblings are described as her heirs. |

The six child interests are expressed as **six sixth-parts of Mary’s one-sixth interest**; the five surviving siblings also account for Elizabeth’s part. This explains a subdivision within this particular branch. It does not resolve the Rochester daughters’ ninths. Mary Black, Robert’s sister, is distinct from Mary Glasco of Rochester, James the carpenter’s daughter. The deed names **Mary Eno Glasgow** as Samuel’s widow, but does not establish Eno as her maiden surname.

### Consequences for Alexander's parentage

The Canadian records now expand **Daniel and Thomas's documented family**, which makes their brothers' and sister's records directly relevant to this enquiry. They still do not name Daniel or Thomas's parents, and they do not establish Alexander-951 as another brother. The Alexander-and-Rosanna tradition remains a hypothesis about Thomas's parents. Alexander's possible place among James's children now has named family and property records to test, but the carpenter's identity with Robert's brother and any connection between his Rochester son and Alexander-951 must each be demonstrated.

The 1861 deed also places wives **Margaret** and **Mary Anne** in the recorded family transaction. It strengthens the identification of the existing Irish couples and gives a later dated occurrence of Daniel's wife before his widowed death in 1871. It does not supply either woman's maiden name or establish the mother of every child. No new Y-DNA result was obtained: documentary linkage to the Prescott brothers expands the family that can be compared with Alexander's paternal line, without proving a genetic match or the joining generation.

### Separate Canadian estate leads

The [bare estate index](https://www.ontariogenealogy.com/uppercanadaontariopioneerwillsestatefiles/leedsgrenvillecountieswillssurrogaterecords/leedsgrenvillecountieswillestateindex.html) entries **Samuel Glasgow, 1875** and **James E., 1900–09** remain unassigned. [Younger Samuel-4021](/people/glasgow-4021.html), two at his next birthday in the 1851 household, is an alternative to the merchant; [James E.-4017](/people/glasgow-4017.html), five at his next birthday, is a specific comparison for the later James E. entry. These are separate from James the carpenter and the Centre Street deeds.

The [1851 Prescott census](https://central.bac-lac.gc.ca/.item/?app=Census1851&op=img&id=e002351566) contains **eight household members, six probable children**. With two later sons reported by local history, eight possible children are accounted for, leaving two of the reported ten unaccounted for by those sources. [Library and Archives Canada fonds R6229-0-0-E / MG24-I39](https://recherche-collection-search.bac-lac.gc.ca/eng/home/record?IdNumber=98738&app=fonandcol) concerns a Niagara farmer who died about 1830 and is excluded as this merchant's archive.

The remaining distinct family groups are Alexander's household; John-867 and Samuel-2908's father-John branch; and the now connected **Kilrea–Lisnagaver–Prescott sibling group**. No record yet joins them under a common parent. The new Irish bridge is established; Alexander's position within that wider family remains the question.

The 2020 correspondent identified a descent through Catherine, described as Thomas and Mary Ann’s sixth daughter, and reported an autosomal match. The supplied message contains no shared-cM total, segment information, checked descent or source for the parent names. Her belief about Thomas’s parents and her separate question about Alexander’s brotherhood are two claims that require separate tests. The reported match is a lead to evaluate for other shared ancestral routes as well as this paternal hypothesis. The correspondence is summarised without publishing the private message or correspondent’s identity.

biography_sections.markdown:
# The Larne connection: a working family reconstruction

**The Larne–Kilwaughter family remains a priority hypothesis for the origin of Alexander's wider paternal family, but the connection is indirect and no record makes it.** Alexander's line shares the Y-DNA branch FT20271 with the line of James J, whose descent from the Kilwaughter family rests on two unproved generations, and the same branch also contains Scottish and Moneymore lines. It is not a father hypothesis: any Larne connection must join above John Glasgow, farmer, Alexander's probable father, and no record names John's father. The useful model connects an Irish branch with a branch that moved to South Carolina in the 1770s. [Robert of Tennessee](/people/glasgow-2769.html), born in South Carolina about 1790–94, is proposed as [James J's](/people/glasgow-2738.html) father. He is not proposed as the father of Alexander, Thomas or Daniel. Their ages therefore supply no objection to that American parentage.

There are two questions to solve together: which older Larne household supplied the Irish branch, and how that branch could join John Glasgow, farmer, Alexander's probable father. [James Glasgow of Larne (Glasgow-1509)](/people/glasgow-1509.html), reportedly born in 1737, is a concrete candidate for the earlier generation. Identifying him with [Glasgow-3905](/people/glasgow-3905.html) means testing whether he was **Adam of Inishrush's father**: 3905 represents that unidentified parental role, rather than a second man established by records. Its placeholder status neither supports nor disqualifies James.

### The American branch has a coherent chronology

| Connection | Evidence and present assessment |
| --- | --- |
| [Robert of Kilwaughter (1143)](/people/glasgow-1143.html) → [James (1144)](/people/glasgow-1144.html), born 1731 | Directly named as father and son in the image-checked [1764 Ballykeel lease](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-33QZ-Y), alongside the congregation-register and Wilson inheritance evidence. The [lease of 13 February 1738/9](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-B99B) independently associates Robert, wife Rachel and James junior; it does not itself call James a son. |
| James → [Archibald (2304)](/people/glasgow-2304.html), about 1769–1818 | James's [1775 will](https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247id_/http://www.lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Paper_JGlasgowWill.html) and the [1817 equity complaint](https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247id_/http://www.lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Paper_Complaint.html) name Archibald among his children. This is a record-supported connection, not merely a tree attachment. |
| Archibald → Robert of Tennessee (2769) | A substantive missing-son hypothesis. The [1800 Newberry household](https://genealogytrails.com/scar/newberry/1800nbycensusG.htm) contains one boy under ten. Archibald's monument-named son James was born about 1806 and cannot be that boy. Robert's early-1790s birth fits. |
| Robert → James J (2738), born about 1809/10 | Both report South Carolina origins; Robert's [1820 household](https://archive.org/details/populationsc18200124unit/page/n21/mode/1up) has a boy aged 10–15, and James later has a documented Giles County land trail. No located record names Robert as James's father. |

The [Kilwaughter chronology](https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247id_/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html) associates James's family with the 1772 Irish petition; his 1775 will places him in South Carolina. These fit the reported 1772/73 migration without proving an exact voyage. If Robert was James J's father, their South Carolina births followed by Robert's [1814 Tennessee militia service](https://scout.lib.utk.edu/repositories/2/resources/4000) fit a later move within America. The Irish collateral branch can have remained in Ireland throughout.

The age fit is stronger when calculated properly. Robert's 1820 and 1840 brackets, combined with Archibald's under-ten boy in 1800, allow **5 August 1790–7 August 1794**, if all three returns concern him and their age bands are accurate. His 1850 age of sixty requires a modest discrepancy; it favours the older end of the working range. That older end also gives a more comfortable fatherhood age for James J around 1809/10. The woman aged 16–25 in Archibald's 1800 household could have been about sixteen to twenty at an early-1790s birth if near the older end of her range. Her age is a constraint to check, not a general exclusion of the family. [Census dates: 1800](https://www.archives.gov/research/census/1800), [1820](https://www.archives.gov/research/census/1820), [1840](https://www.archives.gov/research/census/1840).

This makes Archibald a worthwhile leading named candidate for **Robert's** father. It does not make Robert the uniquely established father of **James J**. [James Glasgow (2439)](/people/glasgow-2439.html), born about 1787, and Sarah form another age-compatible Newberry household. Its 1831 estate should be compared with Archibald's. Robert's Bradshaw Creek associates and James J's district-six land trail still need joining. The [1848 deed](https://tngenweb.org/giles/deed-noah-hancock-to-james-glasgow/) proves James's residence then; its recital of an 1845 title bond proves the earlier transaction, not necessarily residence in 1845.

### James of Larne fits the missing older generation

James was a **Belfast ropemaker** when he took the [1760 Larne ropewalk lease](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-S7XZ-8). That gives the hypothesis a real adult and a property trail near Adam's estimated birth, rather than a name supplied only by a pedigree. The [1773 affidavit](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-M72W-M) says he was over thirty. It supports the older James identity, although the especially good generational fit below depends on his reported 1737 birth.

| Person to compare with James's household | James's approximate age at the reported birth | Evidence for the proposed connection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Adam of Inishrush (3902)](/people/glasgow-3902.html), about 1758 | 21 | A normal father–son interval. Adam's [monument](https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/) names a son James, providing modest naming support. The full child order is unknown; James cannot be called Adam's first son. No record yet joins Adam to the ropemaker. |
| [William (3324)](/people/glasgow-3324.html), about 1763 | 26 | The strongest existing child hypothesis: William's daughter **Jane Shutter** supplies distinctive support for descent from James and Janet Shutter. William's own household is established by the [published monument](https://archive.org/stream/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala_djvu.txt). |
| [John of Inishrush, later Ohio (822)](/people/glasgow-822.html), 1767 | 30 | John and Adam have a substantial Inishrush family association and may be brothers. Making James their common father is an additional hypothesis; John's own naming sequence also supports an alternative older Adam. |
| [Older Alexander (3904)](/people/glasgow-3904.html), estimated about 1770 | 33 | A coherent possible brother of Adam. His own existence and family are reconstructed principally from the later Thomas-parent tradition; no record names James as his father. |
| [Younger James of Larne (3986)](/people/glasgow-3986.html), about 1773 | 36 | An already identified possible son, associated with the 1795 merchant and 1797 junior records. He was earlier considered as a possible father of Alexander; he is now only a weak rival to John Glasgow, farmer (see below). |
| [Robert of Glenleslie (1367)](/people/glasgow-1367.html), about 1779 | 42 | Fits chronologically as another possible child in the broader reconstruction. No record makes him James's son, and he is not securely identified with the Lisnagaver tithe occupier. |

**The 1762 marriage is the main household condition.** It postdates Adam's estimated birth by about four years. If James fathered Adam, Adam could belong to an earlier relationship, a premarital birth, or a chronology needing correction. None is established. Janet Shutter must not acquire maternity merely because she was James's later reported wife. The original marriage and earlier Belfast records could distinguish these possibilities.

Nor does James have to move to Inishrush himself. His [1768 sale](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-DDXW) transferred the ropewalk interest, but [Holmes's 1799 will](https://holmes-history.com/antrim/) still names a James Glasgow, roper, in Larne. An adult son could have moved independently. The ropemaker, the younger [tanner James (3991)](/people/glasgow-3991.html), and the younger merchant must remain distinct record groups; selling a workshop is not evidence of a family migration by itself.

### Possible Larne routes now run through John Glasgow, farmer

Alexander's probable father is John Glasgow, farmer, named as John-867's father in 1846 (see the [parentage comparison](#parentage-context)). Any Larne connection must therefore join above John, not replace him. If Samuel (born about 1789 to 1791 by his 1851 census age and his age at death in 1875) was John farmer's son, as the 1851 "brother" entry implies, John farmer was born about 1770 or earlier. Every link above John is unproved.

| Route above John Glasgow, farmer | Links and how far each is supported | What would settle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The present WikiTree attachment:** [Hugh-1499](/people/glasgow-1499.html) → [John-4179 of Larne](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-4179), married 1769 → John, farmer ([Glasgow-4090](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-4090)) | Hugh → John-4179: possible, on locality and generation only; the Larne monument does not name a son John. John-4179 → John, farmer: unresolved, with no record, and a son of a 1769 marriage would be barely twenty at Samuel's birth. On WikiTree this link carries no uncertain flag. | A Larne record of a son John, or a Rasharkin or Desertoghill record naming John farmer's father. |
| **The ropemaker:** [James-1509](/people/glasgow-1509.html) → John, farmer | Unresolved. James was born before 27 October 1743; nothing names a son John. Chronologically possible only. | The same. |
| **William of Larne:** [William-1505](/people/glasgow-1505.html) → John, farmer | Unresolved, with no record. The older version through [John of Glenleslie (Glasgow-1022)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1022) needs John farmer to be that John, which is disfavoured: his 1851 household records a daughter Nancy who died in 1847 aged 36, while Nancy of Plattsburgh, Alexander's probable sister, lived to 1891. | John farmer's identity and father. |
| **A County Londonderry origin:** the 1796 Desertoghill John, or one of the two Hugh households at Tamlaght O'Crilly in 1740 → John, farmer | That the Desertoghill John is John, farmer, is possible: Samuel's reported Londonderry birth and the 1846 marriage at Garvagh fit, but the Desertoghill residence in the 1846 entry is the bride's. A Tamlaght Hugh as his father is unresolved, on parish-level locality only. | Identity and parentage records for John. |

The earlier routes through older Alexander-3904 and younger James-3986 are withdrawn as routes, because each puts a different father in John's place. Older Alexander and Rosanna remain a weaker rival parent hypothesis; Alexander-3904's birth about 1770 is only an estimate, so chronology does not decide whether he could be John farmer's father. James-3986, reported born about 1773, is too young to be John farmer's father if Samuel was John farmer's son, and barely possible even if John farmer need only be the father of John-867 and Alexander; he remains only a weak naming-based rival. Adam of Inishrush, born 1757/8, is too young to be John farmer's father if Samuel was John farmer's son; the comparison of the ropemaker with Adam is a collateral question.

Hugh, a recurring Larne forename (Hugh-1499, died 1767; the Hugh deceased by February 1843), occurs nowhere among John farmer's probable children or documented grandchildren, so naming gives the first route no support. The absence excludes nothing.

The earlier Adam → older Alexander route compresses the generations: Adam born about 1758 would be twelve at the older Alexander's estimated 1770 birth, while Rose born about 1767 would be three. Moving the older Alexander's birth later and proposing an earlier mother can make Adam's paternity biologically possible, but adds conditions unsupported by records. A brother or cousin relationship is the more natural version to investigate. This chronological preference does not itself prove their kinship.

### Where the DNA and the wider catalogue narrow the search

The [DNA evidence](#paternal-dna) is positive family evidence. Alexander's established descendant line and James J's line share **R-FT20271**, are three steps apart at Y-111 and share DYS714=27. Alongside James J's South Carolina origin and the documented Kilwaughter emigrant family, that makes the Larne connection worth pursuing ahead of an arbitrary same-surname pedigree. The American household evidence was not derived from the DNA, so their agreement is meaningful. But the proposed links from James J to Robert and Archibald are the very links being tested: they cannot also be counted as an independent proof that the match descends from Archibald.

There are already **two additional historical comparison routes** in the [public project](https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview): a reported Robert-1143 line tested at Y-111, and a reported John-822 line tested at Y-67. They place the Larne and Inishrush questions within the same broader STR research network. Their public broad haplogroup labels do not yet establish either as FT20271-positive. Auditing those descent paths and obtaining resolved SNP states would test the proposed geographic connection more directly than treating all current FT20271 matches as interchangeable. John's omission of Alexander from his family Bible weakens **John as Alexander's father**, not John as a collateral relative.

The proposed older Larne tree must also be tested. James-1509’s imported and live attachment is to [William-1505](/people/glasgow-1505.html), while the reviewed catalogue also carries a competing Hugh hypothesis. A William Glasgow, merchant of Larne, witnessed the 1760 lease; his identification with William-1505 needs checking against the other adult Williams. The derivative 1737 baptism names Hugh. [Hugh-1503's](/people/glasgow-1499.html) monument names a different adult son James, born about 1747/48. Both cannot casually be treated as the same child; identifying both as surviving sons of one Hugh would need explanation. William and Hugh's 1736 joint tenancy establishes association, while the proposed connections from them and Robert-1143 to [Robert-1502](/people/glasgow-1502.html) remain unproved. This is the unsettled joining generation, rather than a reason to disregard the well-supported branches below it.

A second origin model remains useful: the two **Hugh Glasgow householders recorded in Tamlaght O'Crilly in 1740**, followed by a parish Hugh in 1772, could represent local continuity behind Adam. John's [Bible](https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1) gives sons Adam–James–John and second daughter Maria, suggesting older Adam and Maria under a conventional naming pattern. That pattern is not fully followed, and applying it to Adam-3902 depends on the unproved brotherhood. These are substantive local alternatives. They prevent treating a good Larne reconstruction as already the only surviving family.

**The research can now be narrower:** test Archibald's missing adult son in estate **647**; test the Larne household through William-3324's surviving **1815 will, D300/1/5/49**, the **1762 marriage** and earlier Belfast records; identify Alexander's immediate family in **CR5/32/1/1/1–2**; and resolve the DNA placement of the specific Larne and Inishrush comparison lines. Each addresses a particular missing connection. The [research priorities](#next-research) explain the outcomes to look for.

## Larne-line assessment — reviewed 21 September 2026

The [archived chronology](https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247id_/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html) reports John Glasgow's 1769 marriage to Rose Allan, now represented by [Glasgow-4179](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-4179). Its c.1745–48 birth estimate is not a baptism. Hugh-1503's memorial and the derivative child list do not name John; this supplies no positive father identification but does not establish an exclusion from an exhaustive family register. Inspect MIC/1B/6 and compare estate/deed succession.

The earlier proposed father–son bridge from this John to a second John born c.1760–70 is unsupported and chronologically awkward: most of the range precedes the 1769 marriage. Establish an actual child or same-person bridge rather than supply an intervening generation. The ropemaker James's parentage and the two James baptism identities remain qualified as in the household discussion above; a chronology's assignment does not resolve them.

The assertion that the two branches must split before 1669 is withdrawn. A reported c.1600 FT20271 estimate for the whole haplogroup does not date the common ancestor of a particular subset. Moreover, James J's links to Robert and Archibald are unproved, and the reported Robert-1143/James-1144 Larne comparison lines are SNP-unresolved in the maintained matrix. [FamilyTreeDNA explains its estimate ranges](https://help.familytreedna.com/hc/en-us/articles/6463932665871-Group-Time-Tree). Neither an eighteenth-century connection nor an older common origin is established.

The [1796 Desertoghill John](https://www.billmacafee.com/1796flaxgrowerslist/1796flaxgrowersderry.pdf#page=49) is a documented flax-premium recipient, but the father identification is unproved. The compiler's [Antrim coverage](https://www.billmacafee.com/18centurydatabases.htm) is selected northern parishes and cannot exclude Larne/Kilwaughter. His two-wheel award records a premium, not an exclusive occupation or genealogical distance.

Priorities remain the original marriage/baptisms, William-3324's 1815 will D300/1/5/49, Killoquin rent roll D3209/1, and tested descent paths for the named Larne comparison lines. The [PRONI pre-1858 Name Search](https://www.proni.gov.uk/name-search) remains relevant; the later Will Calendars cannot exhaust that earlier period.

## John’s uncertain father and corrected marriage — 21 September 2026

[John Glasgow of Larne (Glasgow-4179)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-4179) is now attached to [Hugh Glasgow (Glasgow-1499)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1499) as an **uncertain son**, with low confidence. This is a working hypothesis based on locality and generation, not a record naming his father. [Older William (Glasgow-1505)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1505) remains viable. No mother is attached; Hugh's wife Ann is not thereby identified as John's mother.

The duplicate marriage has been resolved: [Rose Allan (Allan-6611)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Allan-6611) is the wife of the Larne John, married in 1769 according to the [archived Kilwaughter/Larne chronology](https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247id_/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html). Allan-8249 now redirects to Allan-6611, the older ID required by WikiTree. Both Rose profiles cited the same marriage; neither supplied an independent Rose baptism. Her estimated birth about 1750 and inferred County Antrim birthplace remain uncertain. The chronology's 1745–48 birth estimate concerns John, not Rose.

[John Glasgow of West Calder (Glasgow-2846)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2846), son of [John Glasgow (Glasgow-2847)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2847) and [Margaret Anderson](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Anderson-83671), remains a separate identity. Rose has been detached from him. The [1747 Scottish baptism citation](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4T-R5D) has not been re-inspected beyond the existing citation because FamilySearch requires sign-in. No inspected evidence joins that Scottish child to the Larne groom; this separation does not prove that they could never be the same man.

The original PRONI MIC/1B/6 marriage and baptism entries and the named lives in the 1751/1767 endorsements to lease D2977/3A/4/81/72A remain the tests for Hugh versus William. The [Larne memorial](https://archive.org/stream/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala_djvu.txt), pp.47–48, does not name John and is not proved to enumerate every surviving child.

## New original evidence — 21 September 2026

The [20 December 1764 Ballykeel lease](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-33Q6-L), memorial 159661, explicitly names **“Jas Glasgow son of the sd Robt”** on its [continuation](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-33QZ-Y). Robert of Ballykeel/Kilwaughter leased Hugh Shannon half the lower farm, about 31½ acres. Both original images were inspected. This directly strengthens [Robert-1143](/people/glasgow-1143.html) → [James-1144](/people/glasgow-1144.html); Robert's father and the connection to the 1653/1669 householders remain unproved. The third life is Elinor [surname unclear on the saved image; machine-read Jones] otherwise Agnew, the landlord's daughter.

| Further record | New finding and boundary |
| --- | --- |
| [1749 mortgage, memorial 97407](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-7XCG) | Hugh Glasgow, Larne merchant, and Hugh Shutter jointly lent against Old Town property. Strong candidate [Hugh-1499](/people/glasgow-1499.html); no kin stated. This provides an earlier documented Glasgow–Shutter business connection. |
| [1874 deed reciting 1779 and 1832 leases](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77Q4-H) | James Glasgow's 2 October 1779 Newtown lease was renewed to Anne and Jane Glasgow on 25 February 1832. Hugh Glasgow's former tenement bounded it on the west. Title succession is established; the James and women's profile identities and kinship remain unresolved. The monument wife Jane died 1820 and cannot automatically be the 1832 Jane. |
| [1784 lease, memorial 278037](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ4-4SJF) | Image reads **Tanner**, strengthening [James-3991](/people/glasgow-3991.html)'s separate occupational sequence. Sworn 17 August, registered 23 August 1790. The collection label 1734–1736 is misleading for this image. |
| NRS GD154/514–515(c 1653), /525(c 1690), /530(Nov 1692), [/532(1693–1708)](https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD154%2F532&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n) | Exact tenant/rental records located; inspected item descriptions say **Open / On site**. Tenant names and original contents remain unread. These are targeted tests for the early generations, not new Glasgow occurrences. |

The next decisive steps are the Agnew tenant comparisons and the named lives/recitals in the 1736 lease renewals. William's 1815 copy will and Elizabeth's 1824 renewal remain unread. The Belfast captain's 1686 will date does not itself prove death; the 1669 Kilwaughter householder's continuity into 1726 also needs testing.

biography_sections.title: New evidence and competing parentage tests, 29 September 2026
biography_sections.markdown:
**Result: John Glasgow, farmer (Glasgow-4090), remains Alexander's probable father; no direct parent statement has been recovered.** The record-defined father in John-867's marriage, the proposed Desertoghill occupier and the older Glenleslie John are three separate identities. This review does not upgrade a family link or identify Alexander's mother. The tests below reduce some alternatives without turning omissions or uncertain ages into proof.

### A death-week notice missed by exact-name searching

The original **Plattsburgh Sentinel, 6 November 1891, p. 8**, reports Nancy Glasgow's death **at Plattsburgh on 31 October 1891**, aged **about 75**, and her funeral on Monday afternoon at the **Peristrome Presbyterian church**. [Original newspaper page](https://www.nyshistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=plts18911106-01.1.8). The full-page PDF, extracted text and an unaltered crop are preserved under `research/Glasgow-4070/record-excerpts/`.

This independently corroborates the cemetery transcription's death date and identifies the American church context. The reported age suggests birth about **1815–16**, whereas Nancy's own January 1889 will says **about 68**, suggesting **1820–21**. Neither approximate age should be silently replaced by the other. The maintained census indexes give still other ages: 30 in 1860, 50 in 1870 and 65 in 1880 ([MC7C-HHK](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MC7C-HHK), [M8FF-ZQD](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M8FF-ZQD), [MZZF-HDJ](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MZZF-HDJ)). These are not new original-image inspections in this review; they reinforce that neither selected birth estimate is a proved bound. The notice names no relatives or Irish birthplace. The reconstructed Samuel-to-Nancy birth span is consequently about **25–31 years**, subject to all sibling identifications and ages; it does not establish two marriages.

**Search scope:** exact `"Nancy Glasgow"` in the NYS newspaper collection returned 12 pages, largely repeated probate notices; that search missed the death notice. A Clinton County `Glas*` search, 1 October–30 November 1891, returned 53 pages; the first 20 results were reviewed and the 6 November page was then read visually. A Nancy-only Clinton search, 1891–1894, returned 96 pages; only its first 20 were reviewed. These are bounded index searches, not a search of every newspaper page.

{{record:nancy1891-death}}

### Probate: expand the record series, distinguish the generations

The broader [FamilySearch probate catalogue 223236](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/223236), **Probate records, 1790–1969**, contains 19 films and additional minutes and letters series; the narrower will catalogue 319520 alone cannot establish that a petition or later tax report was never filmed. The broader catalogue does not advertise a separate petition-packet or tax-report series. That is a catalogue limitation, not proof that the records do not survive.

The [original Nancy docket](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYCZ-X98?view=fullText), **DGS 005115656, image 34 of 575, volume 6, p. 6**, was visually inspected rather than accepted solely from the AI transcript. It records the 14 January 1892 petition, service by publication, probate and letters on 9 May, a special guardian **for minor heirs**, an inventory and appointment of **Cabell McLean** as collateral inheritance tax appraiser in **March 1894**, and filing of his report on **28 April 1894**. The exact March day and the guardian's name are not confidently read here. The docket does not reproduce the petition, report or a kinship schedule.

The guardian entry is **not evidence that all the cited children were a generation younger**. Nancy's will separately names Robert Wallace Anderson, son of her deceased nephew Robert Anderson, and retains $500 for him until 21. He supplies a concrete younger beneficiary who could explain a guardian, though the docket does not identify the guardian's ward. Nancy also calls him a nephew; the will's terminology must be interpreted against the documented relationship rather than assumed to be perfectly precise. The earlier Robert Anderson and Margaret Kennedy relationships remain the principal explicit kin terms used in the sibling reconstruction.

The G index in the preceding minutes volume, **DGS 005115623, image 12**, was inspected with no Glasgow entry found. A full-text query for `+Glasgow` confined to that DGS returned zero. Neither is an image-by-image search of the volume or a negative search of the complete estate file. Public web searches for Nancy with Walworth/McLean found no independently accessible tax report; no contact or paid retrieval was undertaken.

### Competing explanations and their discriminating tests

| Explanation | Test and result | Present assessment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **One Glasgow father, John farmer, for the probable Nancy sibling group** | Alexander's cited children fit his independently documented family; John-867's James Garvin and Ann fit the separate cited branch; John-867's [1846 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1846/09306/5369439.pdf) names father John, farmer. Known birth surnames in the Dysart, Anderson and McClelland branches are Glasgow. | **Leading, probable.** The common-father inference is economical, but shared surnames alone do not prove full or paternal half-siblinghood. A kinship-bearing sibling record could test it independently of Nancy's petition. |
| **Different Glasgow fathers linked through one mother** | A mother marrying two Glasgow men could preserve all the surnames. No record or identified second marriage supports it. Ordinary maternal-only siblinghood with a differently named father fits the surnames less well. | **Possible, presently unsupported.** It cannot be excluded merely because it needs another same-surname marriage. |
| **Glenleslie John-1022 as father of the whole reconstructed group** | His 1851 return records a daughter Nancy who died in **1847 aged 36**. She cannot be the Nancy who lived in Plattsburgh through 1891. Assigning both Nancys to him requires an unexplained second living daughter of the same name, or a change to the proposed sibling group. [1851 census transcript](https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_072.pdf). | **Disfavoured as a single-family reconstruction.** This does not exclude every half-sibling or collateral connection. John-867's corrected death is **1885**, not 1895; the older age-based objection founded on 1895 must not be reused. |
| **Older Alexander and Rosanna as Alexander-951's parents; Thomas and Daniel his brothers** | Contemporary Canadian deeds prove a Thomas–Daniel sibling family, but do not name Alexander-951. The parent tradition has no inspected contemporary foundation. Their descendants' absence from Nancy's citation remains inconclusive. | **Weaker alternative, not disproved.** An original parent statement for an independently established Thomas–Daniel sibling, plus a bridge to Alexander, is required. |
| **The 1834 Robert occupier as Alexander's father** | Tithe co-occupation does not give age or kinship. If he were the man who died in 1868 aged 71, he would be too young for the normal father model under either Alexander birth estimate; that identity is itself unproved. | **Unresolved tenant identity.** A brother/uncle interpretation remains available; no age can be transferred between unidentified namesakes. |
| **John farmer equals the 1796 Desertoghill flax grower** | Samuel's Derry birth and John-867's Antrim birth fit movement across the Bann, but John's wife and daughter also have Derry births in 1851. County crossings do not date a single permanent move. | **Separate, unproved identity hypothesis.** A tenancy succession, named child or prior residence is needed. |

### Collateral searches that do not depend on correspondence

**Mary Thompson has a new indexed family candidate.** FamilySearch's Scottish civil-registration index records **Mary Thomson, aged 37**, marrying **William Sneddon, aged 45, widower and collier**, on **9 November 1860**, with Mary's parents **Robert Thomson** and **Mary Glasgon Thomson**. [Indexed bride](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:6TLK-6T1J); [indexed mother](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:6TLK-6T1K). Document information gives **008056939_011_M9H1-8LK, image 32**. The image-availability dialog requires a FamilySearch centre or affiliate library; the original was **not inspected**. The older extracted index [XT1H-TBC](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XT1H-TBC) places this marriage at **Old Monkland, Lanarkshire**. Both indexes concern the same event, not independent corroborating marriages. A mother born before about 1805 could belong to Nancy's older sibling generation, but no Irish origin, Nancy relationship or mother's parents have been established. Treat this as a candidate, not an identification of Glasgow-4093.

The existing Mary-4093 biography also reports an unproved Tannybrake widow of William Thompson, dying in 1888 aged 73; its original was not inspected here. If that age is right, she would have been about eight at the Scottish daughter’s c.1823 birth. Keep those candidates separate unless an age or identity correction is established. Mary’s own birth date and birthplace are unestablished; the unsupported catalogue estimate 1874 is withdrawn.

An exact indexed mother-name search for **Mary Glasgow** with child surname Thompson returned six results. These included Anna Thompson, born about 1870, daughter of John Thompson and Mary Glasgow, married at Spokane in 1898, and James Thompson, born about 1880 in Iowa, with the same parental names, married in British Columbia in 1913. They are later-generation alternatives; their common parental names do not prove one family or membership of Nancy's branch. Exact `Glasgon` and `Glasgon Thomson` mother-name variants returned zero in the tested combinations, while a fuzzy Mary Thomson search surfaced the Scottish marriage. This demonstrates why zero exact-name results cannot close the branch.

A follow-up query for daughter Mary with parents Robert Thomson and Mary Glasgow returned only the already located marriage, despite supplied death-year terms; no separate death was identified among the returned records. A strict principal Mary / spouse Robert Thomson / father surname Glasgow query returned zero. Neither result excludes the family: index fields, surname variants and collection coverage remain limitations.

**Lizzie of John's cited branch remains unidentified.** The 1880 West Troy census candidate, Irish-born domestic servant Lizzie Glasgow, aged 21, in James O. Wood's household ([FamilySearch MZCY-D41](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MZCY-D41)), has no inspected parent statement. Public web index searches for Lizzie/Elizabeth Glasgow or Glascow at West Troy/Watervliet and with James Garvin found no independent parentage record. These are index misses, not searches of all civil registers. A namesake remains possible.

**Next independent tests:** follow the Mary Thomson–Sneddon candidate into censuses and death indexes for birthplace and mother's parents; distinguish Ann Glasgow McClelland's own death from her sons' already known parent statements; confirm Robert-938's reported 1902 Scottish death from its original (the 6 January 1892 notice shows he was living when the citation omitted him); examine probate letters/minutes and the 1894 appraisal if accessible. A record naming one sibling's father is more useful than accumulating more neighbouring tenants. The petition is valuable but is not the only route to resolution. No email, message or live WikiTree edit was made in this review.

biography_sections.title: Alexander’s immediate parents: the remaining comparisons
biography_sections.markdown:
**John Glasgow, farmer, is the leading conditional father hypothesis.** It depends on Alexander and John-867 sharing a father within Nancy's probable sibling network. Older Alexander/Rosanna and the Glenleslie family remain unproved; omissions from Nancy's notice do not categorically exclude them. The comparison below preserves the separate evidence for each route.

### The immediate local family tests

| Local explanation | Evidence carrying real weight | Why it does not yet select a parent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **First relationship to resolve: the Thomas–Daniel family**, possibly children of [older Alexander](/people/glasgow-3904.html) and [Rosanna](/people/unknown-761034.html) | Contemporary Lisnagaver households, adjoining later holdings and a repeated Marks witness network establish association. Daniel’s will independently proves Thomas his brother. The [descendant account](https://www.genesreunited.co.uk/boards/board/general_topics/thread/465937) names Thomas’s parents. | No record makes Alexander their brother. Neighbourhood, congregation and holdings overlap as evidence of local association. Applying Thomas’s parent names requires establishing both their historical basis and Alexander’s same-parent relationship. |
| **Parallel household test: the unidentified Robert of Lisnagaver, 1834** | A real local occupier, with a Robert also in the 1836 house list. This is a stronger local lead than an otherwise unconnected pedigree. | Neither his age nor relationship is recorded. Identifying him as [Glenleslie Robert](/people/glasgow-1367.html) is another unproved step, not supporting evidence. He could be a father, brother, uncle or unrelated occupier. |
| **Parallel family test: father John**, named by [John Glasgow of Lisnagaver](/people/glasgow-867.html) | John’s [1846 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063) names father John, farmer; the census calls Samuel John’s brother. | Alexander is not called their brother. Brotherhood alone would not prove both parents were shared. This father is not automatically John of Glenleslie. |

These are research priorities, not numerical odds or mutually exclusive family trees. Robert could be an uncle while Thomas was a cousin. A father not yet identified in the records remains an open possibility.

### What the original Canadian deeds change

The [1861 deed](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWB8-D) now establishes the Canadian connection for Thomas and Daniel: their documented siblings include Robert and Samuel of Prescott, John the watchmaker, Mary Glasgow Black and brother James. [Mary Black’s deed](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQTY-K) identifies six children, including John and Rose Ann of Drumoolish. Their family records now provide a specific local route to the siblings’ parents, independently of the repeated Alexander-and-Rosanna tradition.

The [1868 father statement](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRC-Y) belongs to **Alexander Glasco of Rochester, express agent**, son of James the Prescott carpenter. It cannot be transferred to Alexander-951 without a wife, age, birthplace or migration bridge. The carpenter’s identity with Robert’s brother also remains to be established because the daughters’ property shares do not fit a simple division of the will’s sixth. James is a named family hypothesis to test; the deed has not selected him as Alexander-951’s father. The full [family and property analysis](#family-network) distinguishes the established relationships from these identity steps.

### Evidence that should change the weighting

**The 1868 Robert death could weaken the father hypothesis.** The previously inspected [Ballymoney index](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cidenc-957324) gives age 71, implying birth about 1796–97. If that man were the 1834 occupier, he would have been about **14–15** at Alexander’s c.1811 birth, or **7–8** at the probable death’s c.1804 birth estimate. That is adverse father-age evidence, not confirmation of an older generation. The occupier’s identity is still unknown, so the calculation does not presently exclude him.

**An older Alexander is not required by the tithe.** Alexander-951 could have occupied land in 1834 at about twenty-three, or about thirty under the earlier birth estimate. Gortereagh residence after marriage and omission from the 1836 house section do not prove inheritance or co-residence with a parent. The [land analysis](#record-account) explains the limits of the surviving coverage and acreage comparisons.

**The tradition has less independent support than its repetition suggests.** The public 2020 reply copies the 2007 post; the 2018 pedigree file cites a member tree. The private correspondent believed Thomas’s parent names and separately asked whether Alexander was his brother. Her source is unknown, so neither independence nor copying is established. The clockmaker tradition supplies useful context but misplaces Daniel’s generation if it calls Thomas’s documented brother his uncle. Rosanna’s surname Shaw and reported 1822 death do not become independent evidence for this parentage.

**The genetic family and the immediate father are different levels of the question.** The [Larne analysis](#larne-reconstruction) explains why the wider connection is a priority and compares two routes into Alexander’s generation. The local candidates still need a record or independently traced comparison line that distinguishes their particular families.

### Other immediate-parent candidates and collateral roles

| Hypothesis and present status | Supporting evidence | Contrary or missing evidence; required assumption | Discriminating evidence to seek |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Robert of Glenleslie (Glasgow-1367)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1367): weak | Census age and 1803 marriage permit parenthood | No Lisnagaver bridge; must distinguish him from the tithe occupier | Relationship record bridging the separately documented households. |
| [John of Glenleslie (Glasgow-1022)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1022): weak identity proposal | Nearby father-John model | Age problems; Mary/Maryan ages differ substantially; neither bridge proved | Identify the marriage father; resolve granddaughter identity and her parent. |
| [Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3902): weak as immediate father; useful collateral anchor | Nearby documented family | Monument omits Alexander; unnamed census male cannot identify him | Named-child register or estate record. |
| [Adam (Glasgow-1622)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1622): open, distinct identity | [James's 1851 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3208068) names father Adam | Names no Alexander; cannot merge the two Adams | Identify James and father, then test sibling connection. |
| [John of Inishrush/Ohio (Glasgow-822)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-822): weakened as father; useful collateral and DNA comparison | Relevant documented family | [Family register](https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1) lists nine children, no Alexander | Independent family or church evidence naming Alexander; the two Bible-image inspections are complete. |
| [James of Larne (Glasgow-3986)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3986): weak rival father candidate | Suitable age; Alexander used James twice for sons | Naming and generation only; Larne, not Lisnagaver; a rival to the probable father John Glasgow, farmer, not a link above him (if Samuel was John farmer's son, James, reported born about 1773, is too young to be John farmer's father) | A Lisnagaver or Larne record naming Alexander's father. |
| [Robert of Coltrim (Glasgow-3941)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3941): low priority | Documented older householder | Children unnamed; distinct from Glenleslie and unidentified Lisnagaver Robert | Named family record establishing a bridge. |

The first son’s name James is meaningful family evidence, but it does not identify a paternal grandfather or select the Larne man. Mary/Molly’s parents remain unknown, and James and William McCaheran occur locally. Naming could reflect either side of the family; the surviving child sequence cannot establish a fixed naming rule.

**Retired or excluded:** the imported Robert-and-Catherine parental pair is superseded; Robert’s biological possibility remains separately open. Catherine has no independent maternity evidence. James-1702 is excluded by the maintained chronology; John-1657 is a rejected practical lead in a distinct family. [Detailed candidate sources and exclusions](#parent-candidates) remain accessible.

**For parentage, the first record priority is the family-group material in PRONI CR5/32/1/1/1–2**, alongside the actual source behind the Thomas parent tradition. Extract named households and dated admissions/removals across Alexander’s childhood, rather than another surname-only list. The existing enquiry remains pending. Reconstruct the unidentified Robert and father John in parallel, without merging them into convenient profiles. The [next tests](#next-research) retain the exact references.

Rosanna’s maternity must be assessed separately from older Alexander’s paternity: even paternal half-brotherhood with Thomas would not transfer Thomas’s mother. Mary/Molly’s McCaughan connections concern Alexander’s wife, not his own mother.

biography_sections.title: How the evidence supports this account
biography_sections.markdown:
The account separates the **recorded event**, **the identification of its people**, and **the conclusion drawn from it**. A baptism can directly name a child’s parents while leaving the child’s later identity unknown. A death can have an exact date while remaining a probable match to Alexander. These are different questions and should carry different qualifications.

### How the sources work together

| Source group | Information close to the event | Principal limitation | How it is used here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rasharkin baptisms | Child, named parents, dates and family residence in the maintained transcription | This is a transcription of a register; the incomplete 1838 original has not been inspected | Establishes the early couple and children; missing transcription fields remain missing |
| 1851 original census | One household’s relationships, reported ages, occupations, literacy and marriage years | Birth ages and the 1836 marriage year are retrospective reports; this is not a list of every child ever born | Anchors the household and approximate birth chronology |
| Adult children’s marriages | Bride/groom, residence, spouse and named father | Usually does not name the mother; father details do not by themselves establish that he was alive | Bridges children into adult households using the combined name, place and family evidence |
| Tithe, valuation and revision records | Assessed occupier, holding, lessor and administrative changes | Different surveys, measures and effective dates; tenancy does not establish kinship or ownership | Tracks property associations and tests the Elder succession without inventing an inheritance |
| Civil deaths | Death date, place, reported age/status and informant | Age may be retrospective or uncertain; neither Gortahar death names the other spouse | Supports the death identification through the independently established family network |
| Later traditions, trees and correspondence | What a descendant or compiler reported and when | Copying may create apparent corroboration; an unsourced belief is not a second parent record | Preserves the origins of hypotheses and directs specific follow-up |
| Descendant DNA | Tested genetic relationships, with the panel and result specified | Linking a result to a historical ancestor depends on the descent; mutation evidence cannot fill every documentary gap | Establishes the paternal cluster and tests competing branch arrangements |

An index, a transcription and a tree quoting the same original do not provide three independent confirmations. The surname-project report, STR reconstruction and later discussion can likewise reuse the same genetic observations. Independent civil, church and land records are valuable because they offer different routes through the identity problem; even then, their logical dependencies must remain visible.

### What an unsuccessful search means

Missing evidence is useful only when we know what should have been recorded and what survives. The unnamed 1838 child’s absence from all relevant parts of the household return has more bearing on a survival hypothesis than an unrestricted web search finding nothing. It still cannot establish a death date by itself. A gap in the baptism transcription, a register starting after the marriage, and an archive image requiring onsite access are three different limitations.

The [research history](#research) records completed searches and the wider register of inaccessible originals and unresolved identities; the focused next tests appear below. The next work is prioritised by the proposition it could resolve, not by the number of databases left to search. No numerical parent score is treated as a probability or allowed to replace these source-based arguments.

### Free newspaper search ledger · 30 September 2026

### Sources and coverage

- [News4Clues: New York](https://old.reddit.com/r/Genealogy/comments/18dse19/newspapers_south_to_north_series_new_york/)
  links to [HRVH Historical Newspapers](https://news.hrvh.org/veridian/).
  Its [county browser](https://news.hrvh.org/veridian/?a=p&p=regionbrowser)
  lists Columbia, Dutchess, Greene, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Ulster and
  Westchester. Clinton County/Plattsburgh and Monroe County/Rochester are outside

  links to [Sandusky District Library genealogy](https://www.sandusky.lib.mi.us/genealogy)

  The collection identifies itself as Sandusky, **Sanilac County**, Michigan.
  Searches below cover its entire searchable collection, including cemetery
  entries, histories and obituaries, with no date restriction. This is not a
  comprehensive Tecumseh/Lenawee County newspaper collection.

### HRVH searches

All publications; full text. Quotation marks request an exact phrase; `AND`
requires both terms; `~5` allows words within five positions, according to the
collection's [search help](https://news.hrvh.org/veridian/?a=p&p=help#all).

The broad Nancy results included fiction, other Nancys and references to Glasgow
as a place. Reviewing snippets does not exclude every possible occurrence on
the underlying pages. None of these HRVH results was adopted as genealogical
evidence. The collection's help warns that its searchable OCR can contain errors.

### Sandusky searches

| Query | Search mode | Observed result / inspection |

| `Glasgow` | Words close together | 320 items; first 15 catalogue entries reviewed |
| `James Glasgow` | All words | 246 items; first 15 catalogue entries reviewed; separate words on an issue do not identify a person |

| `Minnie Boland` | Exact phrase | 0 |
| `Minnie Glasgow` | Exact phrase | 0 |
| `Glascow` | All words | 9 items; all displayed titles reviewed; one cemetery entry opened |

The opened **Alex Glascow** cemetery entry gives Lakeside Cemetery, Port Huron,
St Clair County, section F; DOB **9/6/1842**, DOD **10/28/1915**. Those dates are
reported exactly as displayed. This man cannot be Alexander-951 or the
c.1807 Canadian Alexander. The repeated title in the results did not provide an
independent family identification. Record identifier:
`bfcde6e6-c692-4011-b87a-adc61846d131`, collection tote
`5524c4b6-602f-4732-8b31-6a3285eed301`.

The 1966 newspaper hit remains an **uninspected lead**, not a rejected match.
The viewer showed no readable page; direct image viewing and the browser's
asset export did not yield a usable image. Its issue identifier is
`bc793c16-f3ad-4a9c-b942-79fad8d8bc69`, tote
`897f97b8-e88e-4c4d-b452-a136042dfcad`. A late issue can contain historical
material, so its date alone does not exclude relevance. A `James Glascow`
exact-phrase attempt was also submitted, but its completed result was not
captured; it is not counted as a negative search.

### Consequence and remaining work

The new collections are useful supplementary routes, but their coverage does
not close the principal Plattsburgh, Rochester or Tecumseh searches. No identity
or parentage confidence changes. The existing 1891 Plattsburgh notice and 1896
Tecumseh report remain the relevant located newspaper evidence. Nancy's estate
and independent sibling parent statements remain stronger tests of Alexander's
parentage. No correspondence or live WikiTree edit was made.

### Y-DNA testing recommendation — 6 October 2026

Nothing yet places the documented Kilwaughter family inside R-FT20271. Kits 254947 (reported Robert c.1710; Y-111) and B835762 (reported James 1731-1775; Y-37) have no SNP result: the project groups them by STR in its FT25406 group and they display R-M269. Alexander's line and James J's line are both FT20271, but that branch also holds the reported William c.1655 and Robert-12 (Moneymore) lines, and James J's own descent from Kilwaughter has two unproved generations.

**1. First, at no cost.** Through the project administrator, and with the testers' consent, obtain:

- the direct FT6135 call, with coverage, in kit 1002232 (James J) and in the William-c.1655 and James M son-line Big Y kits;
- the paper descent behind kits 254947 and B835762. Robert-1143's only documented son is James-1144, so ask through which of James-1144's sons each runs;
- whether either runs through Archibald, which would make it a test of the James J hypothesis rather than an independent line.

Confirm that each tester is willing to upgrade and that a usable sample is held.

**2. Upgrade kit 254947 to Big Y-700.** If budget allows, upgrade B835762 too, preferably if it descends through a different son of James-1144: agreement between two lines guards against a broken pedigree. A single-SNP or panel test for FT20271, if offered when ordering (not confirmed), is an acceptable screen for inside or outside FT20271 only.

**3. Reading the outcomes**, assuming the testers' reported pedigrees are correct (a disagreement between the two kits points first to a pedigree break):

- **FT25406-positive and FT20271-negative:** the documented Kilwaughter family is outside FT20271. The ancestor shared by Alexander's line and James J's is then not a male-line descendant of Robert-1143, and James J's proposed descent through James-1144 and Archibald is contradicted. Larne men not shown to be Robert-1143's kin (Hugh-1499, William-1505, James-1509) remain untested.
- **FT20271-positive:** the same cluster as Alexander and James J. That is consistent with any route and proves none.
- **FT6135, only if FT20271-positive, and read under a simple inheritance model:** derived places the Kilwaughter line with the Robert-12 lines, with Alexander's line branching earlier; ancestral places it on Alexander's side of that split. Either reading needs James J's own FT6135 call.
- **Private variants:** a new SNP or private variant shared only with kit 1002232 supports James J's Kilwaughter descent, but does not prove Robert-2769 or Archibald as his father or grandfather (Archibald's estate 647 is the record test). A variant shared only with Alexander's line makes that line the Kilwaughter family's nearer relative.

**4. What no result can show.** No result can name Alexander's father or grandfather, confirm John Glasgow, farmer, as his father, or identify which Larne man was the joining ancestor; SNP age estimates carry ranges of a century or more. The Inishrush kit (N18544) is a lower priority. A male-line comparator from John-867 would test the John-farmer brotherhood directly, but none is known.

The public-page placements cited here are summarised readings of 6 October 2026 and should be confirmed on the [project page](https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview) before ordering.

account_sections.title: Mary and the six children
account_sections.markdown:
Begin with **Alexander and [Mary (Molly) McCaughan](/people/mccaughan-222.html)** in the [1851 Lisnagaver census](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=007246523_00175&c19=true). Both were recorded as 40. The marriage columns give us a second anchor:

{{snippets:marriage}}

Their Lisnagaver household contained **Alexander, Mary, Robert (10), James (7) and Ann (4)**. Church and later civil records identify six children in all:

| Child | What the records establish |
| --- | --- |
| [James, born 1837](/people/glasgow-3939.html) | Born 17 January; baptised 9 February 1837. |
| [Unnamed child, 1838](/people/glasgow-3940.html) | A baptism entry; neither a name nor a death is established. |
| [Robert](/people/glasgow-938.html) | Born about 1840–41; married Jane Graham in 1866. |
| [Mary](/people/glasgow-3167.html) | Married Robert Elder in 1871; absent from this census household. |
| [James, born 1843](/people/glasgow-973.html) | Born 9 October 1843; baptised 7 January 1844. The Michigan identification is unproved. |
| [Ann](/people/glasgow-438.html) | Born about 1846–47; married Robert McCracken in 1876. |

[See the household records and children’s later lives](#household).

### What happened to the children?

The Irish relationships are better established than some of the later identifications. Follow each child separately:

{{visuals:children-later}}

**Two Jameses, two records.** The 1837 and 1843 baptisms name separate children. Reuse of the name suggests the first died young, but no death or burial has been found. The unnamed 1838 child is not established as Samuel; neither a forename nor an exact death date can be supplied. The child is no longer presumed to have died young: the 1851 return also omits the living daughter Mary, who may be this child. The transcription has no entries for 1840–41, so Robert’s missing baptism is a coverage gap alongside positive census and marriage evidence. [Baptism transcription](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html) · [Unnamed child’s assessment](/people/glasgow-3940.html).

### A later Elder surname conflict

| Record | Name recorded | What it actually names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1908 birth](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1908/01647/1657700.pdf) | **Samuel Elder** | Mother Jane Elder; no father named. |
| [1911 Gortahar household](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911) | **Samuel Glasgow** | A different surname in the continuing Elder household. |

The census really uses Glasgow. These records do **not** identify Samuel’s father. Inventing a Glasgow father from the surname, then using him to prove the earlier family, would be circular.

account_sections.title: A small Antrim neighbourhood
account_sections.markdown:
The baptisms place the couple at **Gortereagh in 1837–38** and **Lisnagaver by 1843**. Later Elder records lead to **Gortahar**. These are distinct neighbouring townlands; the sources do not date a move precisely.

{{visuals}}

### Which McCaughan family was Mary’s?

The spellings McAughin, McAughern and McCaughan occur in the couple’s records. A compatible surname supplies a lead; each household still needs its own identification.

| Located clue | Why it does not identify Mary’s parents |
| --- | --- |
| William and James McCaheran at **Gortereagh in 1834** | Useful context for the couple’s first baptisms. Neither is called Mary’s father. |
| Mary McCaheren, **22**, with Archibald, **60**, and Elizabeth in Lisnagaver house 31 | A separate younger Mary, potentially the 1855 bride who named father Archy. Alexander’s wife was recorded as 40. |
| Mary McCaheren, **70**, as Margaret Taylor’s mother-in-law | This household relationship does not name Mary Glasgow or her parents. |
| Alexander McCaughan and Cath Quinn’s **1867 Catholic Ballycastle baptism** | A different family; the similar Alexander–Mary names do not connect it to the Presbyterian couple. |

Sources: [Rasharkin baptism transcription](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html), [north Antrim tithe material](https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrimrevisionorder.pdf), and the [maintained household and index comparison](#mary-parentage-research).

**The best remaining manuscript target:** Kilraughts–Dervock society material, **CR5/32A/1**, about **1804–1831**, includes membership and family events. It could name a household around Mary’s probable birth, but has not been inspected. The society divided in 1831, so both contexts matter. [Church-record guide](https://www.americanancestors.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf).

**A tempting clue is the run of Glasgow households in the census.** Read the sequence as separate households, not a family tree:
